This&nbsp;&nbsp; is huge because it really regulates food intake&nbsp; and it's just the beginning. In 10 years, there'll&nbsp;&nbsp; be a whole slew of newer, more potent drugs with&nbsp; fewer side effects. But it shows that you can&nbsp;&nbsp; help people lose weight by taking a medication,&nbsp; when other medications in the past were not very&nbsp;&nbsp; effective and you had to rely on bariatric surgery&nbsp; to get significant weight loss. Now you can get&nbsp;&nbsp; that weight loss with these medications, and it's&nbsp; caused dramatic improvements in people's health.&nbsp;&nbsp; And there might be some weight loss-independent&nbsp; benefits of GLP-1s on the heart. There are weight&nbsp;&nbsp; loss-independent effects where you get beneficial&nbsp; effects of these medications before you lose that&nbsp;&nbsp; much weight — reducing the risk of heart attacks.&nbsp; In the studies where they match the weight loss,&nbsp;&nbsp; the patients who also took the drugs actually&nbsp; did better from a cardiac standpoint, which&nbsp;&nbsp; I'm not sure was expected. The curves diverged —&nbsp; the cardiac effects in high-risk people who took&nbsp;&nbsp; placebo started to spread apart at 6 months. Six&nbsp; months of therapy, you started to get beneficial&nbsp;&nbsp; effects on the heart before much weight loss.&nbsp; And we've seen some data, still unclear,&nbsp;&nbsp; relating to neurological disorders and addiction&nbsp; disorders as well. We had Anna Lembke recently&nbsp;&nbsp; here on the podcast. We find lots of reasons to&nbsp; talk about GLP-1s. Probably nobody whose world is&nbsp;&nbsp; more changed by the advent of these medications.&nbsp; I certainly didn't see this coming even though the&nbsp;&nbsp; science was decades old. Did you see it coming?&nbsp; No, this was really unexpected. It was pretty&nbsp;&nbsp; fast. GLP-1s were first identified in 1987, and&nbsp; then 20 years later, boom — amazing effects.&nbsp;&nbsp; It was being used to treat diabetes — the early&nbsp; ones were short-acting diabetes medications. They&nbsp;&nbsp; increased the dose to get better diabetes therapy&nbsp; and it turned out it caused a lot of weight loss.&nbsp;&nbsp; That hit a light bulb and I thought, there might&nbsp; be some other value here. These drugs stimulate&nbsp;&nbsp; the secretion of insulin, so that's why they were&nbsp; developed for diabetes therapy — weight loss was&nbsp;&nbsp; really a secondary phenomenon. When I initially&nbsp; heard of it, the thought was, it causes nausea,&nbsp;&nbsp; that's why it causes weight loss. But as we've&nbsp; done the studies, we realize that it really does&nbsp;&nbsp; cause dramatic weight loss for many people, and&nbsp; also appears to have these other benefits — food&nbsp;&nbsp; noise, addiction, potentially neuromuscular&nbsp; disease, cardiovascular disease — and not&nbsp;&nbsp; everything can be connected directly to obesity.&nbsp; Even infection. Obesity increases your risk of&nbsp;&nbsp; hospitalized infections, and GLP-1 therapy seems&nbsp; to reduce that risk. Remarkable. I'd love to draw&nbsp;&nbsp; a line then — more fat in general bad, less&nbsp; fat in general good. But you've done this&nbsp;&nbsp; fascinating work with a group who are obese and&nbsp; yet metabolically healthy, and you've started to&nbsp;&nbsp; show some data to try and explain why that might&nbsp; be. Tell us about that work. That's really the&nbsp;&nbsp; key question because obesity is a heterogeneous&nbsp; disease — a real spectrum, like all diseases.&nbsp;&nbsp; At the two ends are people that are obese and&nbsp; healthy, and people that are obese and unhealthy,&nbsp;&nbsp; meaning pre-diabetes, type 2 diabetes, high blood&nbsp; pressure, high liver fat content. Those are most&nbsp;&nbsp; of the people who get those abnormalities. So why&nbsp; does a small percentage of people with obesity&nbsp;&nbsp; not have those diseases? It turns out they have&nbsp; different adipose tissue biology. Their adipose&nbsp;&nbsp; tissue seems to be different from people with&nbsp; unhealthy obesity, and that difference in biology&nbsp;&nbsp; is what we're trying to understand better. They&nbsp; secrete things differently — less of some things&nbsp;&nbsp; than people who have unhealthy obesity — and they&nbsp; secrete some things that are actually healthy and&nbsp;&nbsp; beneficial by comparison. Do you think it's&nbsp; the secreted molecules from the fat that are&nbsp;&nbsp; key to its unhealthiness, rather than just the&nbsp; fact that it exists? It has to be, because how&nbsp;&nbsp; does the fat communicate to other organs? Having&nbsp; bad fat is meaningless unless somehow it tells&nbsp;&nbsp; other organs it's bad or good. It's got to be a&nbsp; communication system — a hormonal type of system&nbsp;&nbsp; that communicates with other organs. That's the&nbsp; key: trying to understand what those mechanisms&nbsp;&nbsp; are, because if you understand them better, you&nbsp; can develop therapies to break the link between&nbsp;&nbsp; excess body fat and metabolic disease. There are&nbsp; some people who have plenty of fat, but it's not&nbsp;&nbsp; signaling in a bad way and they're metabolically&nbsp; healthier. They tend to be women — it's very hard&nbsp;&nbsp; to find men who are metabolically healthy obese.&nbsp; They tend to be women with a lower body fat&nbsp;&nbsp; distribution — large hips, large buttocks, large&nbsp; legs — and not such a large waist circumference.&nbsp;&nbsp; I'd love to go back to the inflammation question,&nbsp; since it's so much in the public domain. You've&nbsp;&nbsp; also measured some pro-inflammatory elements.&nbsp; What are your findings there? Our findings&nbsp;&nbsp; actually go against the dogma of many people.&nbsp; Inflammation — meaning increased immune cells&nbsp;&nbsp; as well as increased expression of genes that are&nbsp; pro-inflammatory — is increased in people with&nbsp;&nbsp; unhealthy obesity. But what's the communication&nbsp; to other organs? We found that the proteins that&nbsp;&nbsp; come out of these adipose tissues from unhealthy&nbsp; people, that are supposed to be pro-inflammatory&nbsp;&nbsp; and causing metabolic harm in other organs, are&nbsp; not different in concentration compared to healthy&nbsp;&nbsp; obesity — except for some. One of the major ones&nbsp; is plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, PAI-1. PAI-1&nbsp;&nbsp; is very important in the cardiology field because&nbsp; of thrombosis and blood clots. And now we're&nbsp;&nbsp; appreciating it's also a very important metabolic&nbsp; hormone that regulates insulin sensitivity. If you&nbsp;&nbsp; have a genetic deficiency in producing PAI-1, you&nbsp; have a lower risk of getting diabetes and heart&nbsp;&nbsp; disease than people with normal PAI-1 production.&nbsp; One of the questioners at the end of your talk&nbsp;&nbsp; asked what I was also interested to ask: many&nbsp; people listening will be wondering, which one&nbsp;&nbsp; am I? Am I one of the metabolically healthy&nbsp; ones? Does that mean I don't need to exercise,&nbsp;&nbsp; or don't need a GLP-1? Can someone going to their&nbsp; doctor get a sense of that by measuring something,&nbsp;&nbsp; and what should they do? How can your work&nbsp; inform precision medicine? The first thing&nbsp;&nbsp; is just what you look like. If you have a large&nbsp; waist, a beer belly, you're more prone to have&nbsp;&nbsp; unhealthy obesity. If you have large hips and legs&nbsp; and not much of a belly and you're a woman, you're&nbsp;&nbsp; much more likely to have healthy obesity. Then a&nbsp; doctor's regular blood test — triglyceride levels,&nbsp;&nbsp; HDL cholesterol, blood glucose, and blood pressure&nbsp; — will all identify people that are metabolically&nbsp;&nbsp; unhealthy. Jerry Reaven described this early on&nbsp; as Syndrome X, which is now called the metabolic&nbsp;&nbsp; syndrome. That can be identified on a routine&nbsp; clinical exam. But we know the cut points are&nbsp;&nbsp; artificial — everything is a spectrum — and&nbsp; even high-normal is unhealthy. A high-normal&nbsp;&nbsp; blood pressure is unhealthy compared to a lower&nbsp; blood pressure, and a high-normal glucose like 90&nbsp;&nbsp; is not as healthy as a glucose of 75. What about&nbsp; HbA1c? That's the long-term glycated hemoglobin,&nbsp;&nbsp; the ultimate test for where your glucose level has&nbsp; been over several weeks. That's another important&nbsp;&nbsp; measurement that might become part of the routine&nbsp; clinical exam. A high HbA1c also helps determine&nbsp;&nbsp; healthy versus unhealthy obesity. The normal&nbsp; cut point of 5.6 or lower is not really "so&nbsp;&nbsp; normal" unless you're down around 5.0 or 5.1. The&nbsp; high-normal in that range is also not so healthy.&nbsp;&nbsp; In medicine, we always have our 95th percentile&nbsp; population norms, and depending on the lab,&nbsp;&nbsp; they may be derived from thousands of patients —&nbsp; but often from quite a small number for certain&nbsp;&nbsp; assays — and from a population that's never&nbsp; particularly well described and is probably&nbsp;&nbsp; not that diverse. There's been some work recently&nbsp; suggesting that your own personal normal, measured&nbsp;&nbsp; over several years, might be a better guide.&nbsp; Speaking as someone without a completely normal&nbsp;&nbsp; HbA1c, I wonder if my measurements from my 20s,&nbsp; 30s, and 40s, if they were all the same as today,&nbsp;&nbsp; would be truly meaningful versus where I am on a&nbsp; population scale. How do you think about that? You&nbsp;&nbsp; have to think about obesity-related metabolic&nbsp; diseases as a constellation of diseases that&nbsp;&nbsp; track together. If you have one abnormality but&nbsp; everything else is good, you're not at the same&nbsp;&nbsp; risk as someone who has that same abnormality plus&nbsp; these other abnormalities. If you're a runner, fit&nbsp;&nbsp; and healthy, and you have a slightly high HbA1c,&nbsp; but your triglycerides are low and your HDL is&nbsp;&nbsp; high — that's not the same as someone with a high&nbsp; HbA1c who also has those other risk factors. What&nbsp;&nbsp; we often do is focus on individual organs instead&nbsp; of the multi-organ system, which really determines&nbsp;&nbsp; your health. One of our new programs here in the&nbsp; Department of Medicine at Stanford is thinking&nbsp;&nbsp; about metabolism because it touches on so many&nbsp; of our historically divided subspecialties — but&nbsp;&nbsp; in reality, it touches on all of them. Treatments are&nbsp;&nbsp; also often the same for all the different&nbsp; organs. - What is the future of obesity care? | Melanie Jay, MD, MS | TEDxNYU Langone Health: Kind: captions Language: en Transcriber: To Thi Mong Kieu Reviewer: To Kiet Tuong B How do we know if we are living in a miracle moment? And if we are, what should we do? On July 27th, 2023, I received an email asking me if I wanted to be interviewed by Oprah Winfrey for a special she was doing about obesity. It is an incredible time to be a physician scientist specializing in obesity, after decades of struggling to improve the health of our patients. We finally have effective new medications for this disease until 2023. My research focused on the care of obesity was only published in academic journals. Each of those 90 plus papers reflected up to eight years of work and were rarely seen by the patients or by the public. But being interviewed by Oprah was a powerful opportunity to reach a much larger audience. Oprah led me and three other obesity experts through an insightful conversation about the new medications and what they mean for patients. We listened as members of the studio audience recounted how they overcame obesity stigma and were finally able to manage their disease. And then Oprah asked me a question. Are these drugs a miracle moment? Is this a miracle moment we are having? I was stumped. I felt overwhelmed as my 20 years of grappling with difficult problems with obesity care flashed before my eyes. And so I said no. When I went to medical school, there were a few medications to treat obesity. Bariatric surgery, which involves making the stomach smaller and often shortening the intestines was, and still is, the most effective treatment. I was taught that if patients were just more motivated to eat less and move more, then they would lose weight. I had no idea how this belief creates negative attitudes towards people living in larger bodies, with potentially deadly consequences. In 2003, when I was a resident, the emergency room staff evaluated a lovely woman in her 40s who was very nervous and thought she had the flu. She was over £350, so it was difficult for the doctors to hear the pneumonia in her lungs. Her blood pressure cuff was too tight for her large arms, making her blood pressure seem higher than it actually was. She didn't want to complain or take up too much space. When I came to evaluate her, I was told that she was stable and she'd be counseled to lose weight. But something didn't seem right. So instead of discharging her, I started the process of admitting her for observation. Over the next hour, her blood pressure went low. She became dizzy and short of breath, and then her blood pressure went lower. We rushed her to intensive care, where we found she had sepsis and it was a miracle she didn't die. Over 60% of people with obesity say they experience stigma in health care, which can make them avoid going to see the doctor. Also in 2003, I learned that the rate of obesity had doubled in 20 years and was 32%. It is now 42% determined to make a difference. I co-founded Bellevue Weight Management Program with fellow residents. That still exists. Ours was the first of its kind in a safety net hospital, but I quickly became discouraged as my patients would lose weight initially only to gain it right back. My struggles to treat obesity made me want to research it. Unlike then, we now recognize that obesity is a disease. It is partly caused by genetics and is as heritable as height. Our genes interact with environmental factors, leading to weight gain and obesity. Environmental factors include things like food deserts, lack of safe spaces for physical activity, stress, medications, pollution, and a whole host of other things that are more common in vulnerable communities. Obesity can impact almost every part of our bodies and causing medical complications in almost every organ system. But it is hard to lose weight. Why? Well, our brains regulate weight like a thermostat, creating a sort of weight set point. So when we try to lose weight by eating less, what happens? Well, our hunger hormones go up so we feel hungrier and our ability to cut calories goes down so we burn less calories. And this is why patients often regain the weight back to where they started. The new medications containing G one receptor agonists with names like semaglutide, tirzepatide, wegovy, ozempic, and ssep bound signal to the brain that we aren't hungry and allow people to remain at a lower weight set point. My little sister Lauren went to Weight Watchers when she was ten years old. As a young adult, Lauren struggled with bipolar disorder and had a few manic episodes that were very disruptive. Her psychiatric medications stabilized her, but also caused a £50 weight gain, leading to medical problems and pain. Diligent lifestyle change did not work long term. Years later, when she went on semaglutide, her weight, blood pressure and glucose came down. Her back pain went away and she was able to exercise. The combination of her psychiatric and obesity care medications have been miracles for her. But not everybody has the same success as Lauren. Over 60% of people stop taking obesity care medications at one year, often due to the $500 or more costs per month that aren't covered by insurance. But costs don't explain fully why people stop. Patients often need more support to manage lifestyle change and also to manage side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and constipation. When my patient Josie got injured and started eating at the Wendy's closer to his home, he could no longer tolerate semaglutide because the medications made him too sick. Another reason why people stop is because they don't see obesity as a chronic disease. So once they lose weight, they go off the medication. And just as blood pressure goes up, when we stop hypertension medication weight goes back up when we stop obesity care medication. And I worry about the major disparities in who can access obesity care medications. Those who are affluent can buy them, but some of my most vulnerable patients cannot. All the ads on TV and social media are appealing to society's celebration of ideal body types, and this has led to dangerous counterfeit drugs, bogus herbal supplements and compounding pharmacies offering cheaper, less regulated versions of obesity, care medications and obesity. Stigma has hit close to home, as Lauren is often told that she should have lost weight the natural way. We don't say this about any other chronic disease. Would you ever tell somebody with diabetes that they should only manage their dangerous blood glucose levels the natural way, without the help of essential medications? And yet, despite all these problems that flashed before my eyes when I was with Oprah, I now believe that we are in a miracle moment for obesity care. For the first time in my career, Lauren and many of my patients can achieve better health outcomes. The medications can prevent diabetes and heart attacks. They can improve liver disease, kidney disease, and sleep apnea. And there are many new medications being developed that could be approved soon, that could provide even more options and benefits to patients. Stories and experiences like Lauren's are finally starting to convince people that obesity is not about lack of willpower. Obesity is a disease. So there are now three big things that we all need to do. First, fund obesity research. We have so much more to learn about how to both treat and prevent obesity, with recent threats to healthcare and research funding. This is all the more urgent. Second, improve access to obesity care, including lifestyle, including medications, including surgery for all patients who need it. And finally, and this is something that each of you can do right now. And obesity stigma and treat obesity like the chronic disease that it is. I'm learning that miracle moments are transformational. They are the best time for us to achieve and for us to solve our most difficult problems. 22 months ago, when Oprah asked me if we are in a miracle moment, I said no. But if anyone asked me again, I will say yes, and that now we must seize this moment to transform obesity care. Thank you.

- Role of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists for Weight Loss: Kind: captions Language: en [MUSIC PLAYING] LEE-SHING CHANG: Hi. My name is Dr. Lee-Shing Chang. In this video, we'll be talking about GLP-1 receptor agonists and their use in weight loss. Key takeaway points from this video are to understand the major trials establishing GLP-1 receptor agonists' efficacy for weight loss. When thinking about weight management, there are five medications that have been FDA approved for long-term weight management as of 2021. Of these agents, orlistat works by decreasing the digestion and absorption of fats at the level of the gastrointestinal tract. The other agents work in large part by regulating appetite at the level of the central nervous system. Two of them, liraglutide and semaglutide, are GLP-1 receptor agonists. We'll focus on these two agents in this video. Of note, there are multiple other GLP-1 receptor agonists that are available for use, all of which are associated with weight loss. However, only two, liraglutide and semaglutide, have specific FDA indications for long-term weight management. GLP-1 stands for Glucagon-Like Peptide 1. GLP-1 is an incretin hormone produced by the L cells in the intestine in response to food intake. GLP-1 has multiple effects. And GLP-1 receptors are found throughout the body, including in the brain, the gastrointestinal tract, the pancreas, and other organs. GLP-1 has numerous actions. From a weight loss and metabolic perspective, the most relevant actions are that it helps regulate appetite and lower glucose. GLP-1 is thought to act at the hypothalamus, regulating appetite by increasing satiety. GLP-1 also acts on the gut to slow gastrointestinal motility and to increase satiety. And it also acts on the pancreas to upregulate insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. Liraglutide and semaglutide share over 90% homology to native GLP-1. Both liraglutide and semaglutide have been modified to irreversibly bind to serum albumin in the body. This increases their half-life. Both liraglutide and semaglutide were initially approved as glucose-lowering medications for use in type II diabetes. However, both have been found to induce significant weight loss in many individuals. Dedicated trials in individuals with overweight and obesity without type 2 diabetes have confirmed their efficacy for weight loss in nondiabetic populations. The SCALE trial established liraglutide's efficacy in weight management. It was a double-blind, randomized controlled trial comparing liraglutide at a dose of 3.0 milligrams given subcutaneously once a day to placebo in just over 3,700 patients without type 2 diabetes and with a BMI either of at least 30 or of at least 27 with concurrent dyslipidemia or hypertension. Both groups also received lifestyle modification counseling. After 56 weeks, patients in the liraglutide group lost a mean of 8.0%, or 8.4 kilograms, of their body weight, compared to 2.6%, or 2.8 kilograms, in the placebo group. The STEP trials are a series of trials to study semaglutide's efficacy in weight management. STEP 1 was a double-blind, comparing semaglutide 2.4 milligrams once weekly given subcutaneously to placebo. It enrolled just under 2,000 patients and, similarly, with a BMI of at least 30 or of at least 27 with at least one weight-related coexisting condition. Both groups received lifestyle intervention. After 68 weeks, patients in the semaglutide group lost a mean of 14.9% of their body weight, compared to 2.4% in the placebo group, for an estimated treatment difference of 12.4%. More participants in the semaglutide group than in the placebo group achieved weight reductions of 5%, 10%, and 15% or more at week 68. For example, for weight reductions of at least 5%, the comparison was 86% in the semaglutide group versus 32% And 51% of participants lost 15% or more weight, compared to only 5% in the placebo group, the takeaway point being significant weight reduction was seen with use of semaglutide once weekly. If you're wondering whether liraglutide or semaglutide is more effective for weight loss, the STEP 8 trial helped to answer that question. The STEP 8 trial randomized 338 participants to semaglutide with matching placebo or liraglutide with matching placebo. Participants did not have diabetes and had a BMI of at least After 68 weeks, the primary outcome showed significantly greater weight loss with semaglutide compared to liraglutide. The mean weight change from baseline was 15.8% with semaglutide, versus 6.4% with liraglutide, for a treatment difference of 9.4%. An important note is that continued use of GLP-1 receptor agonists is needed to support maintenance of weight loss. In the STEP 4 trial, after semaglutide run-in period of 20 weeks, participants were randomized to either switch to placebo or to continue semaglutide. As you can see here, those who switched to placebo saw a regain in weight, compared to those who continued semaglutide, who continued to lose weight with continuing semaglutide. - ‘Maintenance’ doses of GLP-1 medication | Ohio State Medical Center: Kind: captions Language: en-US One of the things that I'm looking forward to over the coming years in the field of obesity medicine is the development of new therapeutic agents for the management of obesity as a chronic disease. We know right now that the two medications that are available that are GLP-1 receptor agonists — semaglutide and tirzepatide — both have what are considered maintenance doses available. And these are the dosages that patients ideally would achieve by an upped titration schedule. And then working with their physician [it] can be determined which of these doses is the best long-term dose for them to continue on. I think that being able to have these maintenance doses is very important, because we know that each person is going to have a different response to these medications. Some patients may lose a good bit of weight on a lower dose and other patients may need to escalate all the way to the highest dose before they're really achieving meaningful weight loss. So having these off ramps for patients to get off of that escalation schedule&nbsp; and maintain their dose is important. With semaglutide, we know that the two approved maintenance doses are the 1.7mg dose and the 2.4mg dose. For tirzepatide the approved maintenance&nbsp; doses are 5mg, 10mg, and 15mg. For patients that are considering using the lower doses of these medications, I think it's very important if the plan is to use just a lower dose and then to discontinue therapy without achieving a maintenance dose and without being, again, maintained on a maintenance dose — it's really important for these individuals to consider other options for weight loss. Again, we know that the risk of weight regain when stopping these medications is high even if you are utilizing a lower dose. So again, I'm hopeful over time as more options hit the market there will be medications that are going to hit that sweet spot for patients, where they'll be able to take the lowest effective amount of medication needed to be able to maintain the weight that they ideally need to lose.

Those reductions began rolling out in late 2025 after pressure on drug makers to bring US cash prices closer to international levels. So, trumprx did not introduce new GLP-1 savings. It launched by displaying prices that drug companies had already put in place. Trumprx itself does not sell medication. It is not a pharmacy. It does not process prescriptions. Instead, it functions as a price information platform powered by data from GoodRx, showing estimated cash prices at participating pharmacies and manufacturing partners. When patients use those prices, they are paying fully out of pocket. The costs do not go through insurance. They do not count towards deductibles, and they do not count towards out-of-pocket maximums. For GLP-1 users, that distinction matters. Many patients who had already enrolled in manufacturer programs before Trump Rx launched were already paying the same amounts now being promoted on the site. What Trump Rx mainly did at launch was centralize that existing information and place it under a government-branded platform. That can improve visibility and make discounts easier to find, but it did not represent a new round of price cuts for Zempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, or Mounjaro. It also did not change insurance rules, prior authorization requirements, supply limits, or long-term pricing strategies that continue to affect access to these drugs. And story number eight, for people living with diabetes who have already experienced serious limb complications, new research suggests that medication choice may make a life-changing difference. A new study published in JAMA Network Open finds that patients treated with GLP-1 medications had significantly lower risks of repeat amputations, heart problems, kidney failure, and death compared with patients taking older diabetes drugs. Doctors have long known that once someone with diabetes experiences a major limb event, such as a severe ulcer or an amputation, their long-term health risks rise sharply. These patients face much higher chances of future amputations, heart disease, and kidney failure. But until now, there has been limited evidence showing which treatments best protect people in this high-risk group. Researchers addressed that gap by analyzing nationwide health data from Taiwan spanning more than a decade. They studied more than 17,000 patients with diabetes who had already experienced major limb complications. Some patients were treated with GLP-1 medications. Most were treated with another common class of drugs called DPP-4 inhibitors. The researchers then tracked what happened to these patients over time. The results were striking. Patients taking GLP-1 medications had about a 10% lower risk of repeat limb events and a 14% lower risk of amputations. They also had a 38% lower risk of major heart problems and a 43% lower risk of cardiovascular death. Overall mortality was 37% lower. The risk of needing long-term dialysis was nearly 40% lower. In other words, these medications were linked to better outcomes across limb health, heart health, kidney function, and survival. The study suggests that GLP-1s may offer far more than blood sugar control, especially for patients already dealing with advanced complications. For people who have lost part of a limb or suffered severe circulation problems, these drugs may help reduce the risk of even worse outcomes in the future. The authors say the consistent benefits across multiple organ systems support using GLP-1 medications as preferred option for secondary prevention. That means protecting patients who have already been through serious complications, not just trying to prevent the first one. This was a retrospective study, meaning it analyzed existing data rather than assigning treatments in a clinical trial. So, it can't prove cause and effect, but the size of the study and the consistency of the findings make it an important piece of evidence for doctors and patients to consider. For people living with diabetes, especially those who have already faced amputations or serious limb damage, this research reinforces something we talk about often. Medication choices matter, access matters, and long-term outcomes depend on more than just today's blood sugar reading. This is about protecting quality of life, independence, and survival. I mean, so those are big numbers. I mean, it Yeah, like 40% You definitely want a GLP-1 if [snorts] you've had these diabetes and amputation issues. You would definitely want to be on a GLP-1 according to those retrospective numbers. I'm no doctor, but I'd sure sign up for it. I think you're absolutely right. Story number nine, new real-world data is adding to growing evidence that GLP-1 medications work best when they're combined with consistent behavioral support and habit building. A new report from Noom analyzed outcomes from 14,203 members enrolled in its GLP-1 RX program between December 2024 and February 2025. All participants logged their weight and activity during the study period. Researchers followed participants for 40 weeks and compared outcomes based on how actively users engaged with Noom's behavioral tools, including tracking, educational content, and daily coaching features. The results showed clear differences. Members in the highest engagement group lost 25.2% more weight on average than those in the lowest engagement group. Highly engaged participants also remained medication programs 2.2 times longer than those who were less engaged. That matters because medication persistence is one of the strongest predictors of long-term success on GLP-1 therapy. The analysis also found that more engaged users were more likely to maintain regular dosing schedules and fewer interruptions in treatment. Noom CEO Geoff Cook said the data shows that medication and behavioral support reinforce one of reinforce one another and that sustained engagement is closely tied to better outcomes. The findings are consistent with similar results reported by other digital health providers, including Ro and Omada Health, which have published data showing improved weight loss and adherence when GLP-1 therapy is paired with structured coaching and behavioral programs. Across these programs, patients who regularly track behaviors, engage with educational tools, and receive ongoing support tend to lose more weight and stay on treatment longer than those who rely on medication alone. Researchers and clinicians say this reflects how GLP-1 medications work in real life. The drugs help regulate appetite, blood sugar, and hunger signals, but they do not automatically create routines, improve food choices, manage stress, or establish consistent patterns of behavior. Those changes come from the patient. Because of that, experts increasingly view GLP-1 therapy as most effective when it is combined with systems that support accountability, education, and daily engagement. It's also important to note that Numes' analysis was observational. It did not randomly assign participants to different engagement levels, which means it cannot prove that engagement alone causes better results. However, the large sample size and consistent pattern strengthen the evidence that behavior and adherence play a major role in outcomes. For people using GLP-1s, the practical takeaway is clear. The medication changes the biology, but habits determine how well that change translates into lasting results. Patients who stay engaged, monitor their behavior, and build structure around their treatment are more likely to maintain progress over time. As more long-term data emerges, researchers say the focus on obesity treatment is shifting from medication alone to integrated care models that combine pharmacology with behavioral support. one thing worth adding for anyone in the comments who wants a little more depth on the mechanism: glucagon-like peptide-1 is an incretin hormone, meaning it gets released from your gut in response to food and its job is basically to coordinate your body's glucose response. it signals the pancreas to release insulin only when blood sugar is actually rising, tells the liver to slow down on releasing stored glucose, and also sends satiety signals to the brain. the "agonist" part just means the medication mimics that hormone and binds to the same receptors, so you're not adding something foreign to the system, you're amplifying a pathway your body already uses

- How to Suppress Your Appetite and Naturally Boost GLP-1: Kind: captions Language: en "How to Suppress Your Appetite and Naturally Boost GLP-1" About 20 years ago, there was a discovery that would forever change our ideas about fiber: Our gut bacteria eat the fiber we eat to produce important signaling compounds called short-chain fatty acids. But before I get carried away, a little science lesson to frame the discovery. Cells are the fundamental unit of life. We’re composed of trillions of them. They communicate with each other through receptors on the surface of our cells. That’s how many hormones work; it’s like a lock and key. Hormones are signaling messengers, each with a unique shape. When released into the bloodstream, they circulate through the body until they find a receptor they can fit into. Once the key is in the lock, it can turn on or off a whole series of reactions in the target cell. The largest family of cell receptors is known as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs, for short). More than a third of the drugs currently on the market work by plugging into these receptors. That’s how drugs like antihistamines work. We’ve discovered hundreds of different GPCRs, but, remarkably, we don’t yet know what many of them do. We have the lock; we just don’t know what key fits. Accordingly, they’re called "orphan" receptors. Two of these mystery receptors, known only as GPR43 and GPR41, were found heavily expressed throughout the body in our immune and fat cells, and in our gut, muscles, and heart. We knew they must be vital, but we didn’t know what activated them until 2003, when they were "deorphanized" (that’s actually what scientists call it). The keys that fit into those important locks were the short-chain fatty acids that our gut bacteria make when we feed them fiber. This is how our gut bacteria may communicate with us. Renamed free fatty acid receptors, their existence is now considered crucial insight into how fiber could play such an important role in so many of our chronic diseases. Hormones are defined as signaling messengers produced in one organ that circulate through the bloodstream and have a regulatory effect on another organ. So, these short-chain fatty acids can be considered hormones. It’s just that the organ that produces them is our microbiome, the bacteria that populate our gut. They can’t make these hormones, though, without fiber. What do the free fatty acid receptors on our fat cells do? Remember leptin, the hormone produced by fat cells that helps tell our brain how to regulate our body weight? Short-chain fatty acids stimulate the production of leptin. This can be demonstrated in a petri dish with individual fat cells, or by using fat tissue samples removed during surgery. Drip on some and leptin production almost doubles. Leptin is an "anorectic" hormone, so-called because it generates a loss of appetite and weight, but it does so over the long term. Leptin levels slowly rise as the volume of body fat gradually increases. There are other anorectic hormones that instead work rapidly, signaling our brain on more of a meal-to-meal basis. Two of these short-term appetite suppressants are PYY and GLP-1, which are both secreted by specialized L cells that line our colon. Guess what receptors are crowded all over their surface? Free fatty acid receptors. Drip some short-chain fatty acids onto L cells and they start churning out PYY and GLP-1. You can do this in a petri dish or in a person, either by infusing their rectums with a short-chain fatty acid enema or the old-fashioned way, by feeding people fiber, or even better, fiber-rich foods, like this whole rye kernel wheat bread. These hormones then get released where they can shoot up into the appetite center of our brain and turn down our cravings. The flipside is ghrelin, the so-called hunger hormone. Ghrelin levels rise in our blood before a meal to stimulate our appetite, and fall down again once we eat, before slowly building back up to drive us back to the kitchen. But four hours after eating just 24 grams of fiber, people’s ghrelin levels are suppressed as much as if they had just had 500 calories’ worth of food. Longer studies show similar effects. 11- and 12-year-old children with overweight or obesity who were randomized to increased fiber intake for 16 weeks ended up eating hundreds of fewer calories of a buffet meal, compared to the placebo control group.

  2. @aboutsupplies [6 likes]: If the mechanism were true in the universal, causal way the video implies, several downstream predictions would have to hold with consistency across human physiology. 
They don’t. Here is the systematic breakdown.

If SCFA-driven GPCR activation were the dominant regulator of appetite, then:

* Individuals on zero-fiber ketogenic or carnivore diets would exhibit chronic hyperphagia. They do not. Many report the opposite: spontaneous hypocaloric intake and appetite suppression despite producing negligible colonic SCFAs.
* Controlled feeding trials of low-carb, low-fiber diets would show increased appetite and weight gain. They don’t. Multiple trials report reduced hunger scores and reduced ad libitum intake even when fiber is nearly absent.
* Bariatric-level appetite suppression from ketosis could not occur, because the mechanism bypasses SCFA–GPCR signaling entirely.

If leptin production from SCFAs were a major, long-term regulator of body weight, then:

* Higher-fiber populations would demonstrate higher circulating leptin at equivalent body fat levels. They don’t. Leptin tracks fat mass, not fiber fermentation.
* Leptin resistance could not occur in high-fiber individuals, but it does.
* Leptin levels in low-fiber populations (Inuit, Maasai, contemporary keto or carnivore adopters) would be dangerously low or dysregulated. They aren’t.

If SCFA-triggered PYY and GLP-1 release were meaningfully suppressing appetite, then:

* Removing fermentable fiber should sharply reduce PYY/GLP-1 responses. It doesn’t. Protein, fat, and mechanical stretching of the stomach induce PYY and GLP-1 without any reliance on colonic SCFAs.
* High-fiber meals would reliably outperform high-protein meals for satiety in controlled trials. They don’t. Protein remains the most potent macronutrient for satiety.

If fiber-induced ghrelin suppression were a dominant mechanism, then:

* Fiber-free diets would cause elevated ghrelin and persistent hunger. They don’t. Ghrelin drops sharply on ketogenic and carnivore diets.
* Ghrelin would rise predictably when fiber is removed. Trials show the opposite: ghrelin often decreases as carbohydrate intake falls, independent of fiber.

If fiber reliably caused “hundreds fewer calories” of reduced intake, then:

* Fiber-supplementation trials would produce strong, consistent weight-loss effects. They don’t. Meta-analyses show modest or null results unless accompanied by overall dietary change.
* Replacing calories with pure fiber supplements would reduce body weight independent of diet composition. Trials show weak effects at best.

If the system operated as a universal appetite-control circuit, then:

* Populations with extremely high SCFA production (e.g., agrarian Africans) would exhibit chronically suppressed appetite and extremely low intake. They don’t. SCFA production correlates with diet pattern, not with pan-human anorectic signaling.
* High-fiber diets would outperform all others for long-term weight loss. They don’t. Low-carb, low-fiber diets routinely match or outperform them, driven primarily by protein leverage, stable insulin dynamics, and reduced hedonic drive.

Systematic bias check:
The video assumes:

* Fiber → SCFA → GPCR → appetite control is the central axis. Physiologically false. Appetite is regulated by protein leverage, neurochemical reward circuits, insulin dynamics, ketone signaling, mechanical distension, and energy status.
* Findings from cell and receptor biology scale cleanly to real-world eating behavior. They rarely do.
* Correlational outcomes in fiber-rich populations reflect fiber causality rather than overall diet pattern, food reward level, or energy availability.
* Absence of fiber implies absence of appetite regulation. Carnivore and strict keto populations contradict this assumption directly.

Conclusion:
The described mechanisms exist, but their causal weight is overstated. If they were the dominant levers of appetite, the empirical world would look radically different.

- You're Being Lied To About Ozempic | Truth Complex | Business Insider: Kind: captions Language: en-US In just a few years, Ozempic has become a household name and a cultural phenomenon. GLP-1 drugs are everywhere, and already one in eight US adults have tried them. The Danish company that makes Ozempic is worth more than The Coca-Cola Company and McDonald's combined. Look online, and you'll see comments about "Ozempic face," hair loss, severe stomach problems, and dangerous side effects. And then a moment later you'll see a report that it could help with fertility or treating Alzheimer's or even shopping addiction. And it's not just weight-loss drugs. We've been lied to about weight loss itself for years now. How much do we know about GLP-1 drugs? And are we being told the full truth about them? I've spent the last few months diving into the research and even tried to get some GLP-1 medication myself to see what's really going on here. At this point, I spent a lot of time on social media digesting what the discourse is out there about this medication. One of the pieces of misinformation I'm seeing over and over again is this idea that these drugs are brand new, that they're not well studied, and that they're not well understood. It's not studied for this. You know, there's no studies on what it does to a body without diabetes. There is no research, no research, on a person that is not diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. So, we know that this line that they're untested or not understood is just not true. They've been studied a lot for both safety and efficacy for both diabetes and weight loss. Thousands of people have been studied in clinical trials specifically for obesity but not for diabetes. The new phenomenon is that Ozempic is a household name, and it became a household name because of its weight-loss effects. However, it's part of a class of drugs that have been used for decades to help people with type 2 diabetes regulate their blood sugar. And just in that regard, it's been a huge medical breakthrough. I think we could probably critique that on its own in that our society is so weight-obsessed that none of these diabetes treatments were a household name even though a million and a half people die of it each year, but as soon as it started making celebrities skinny, all of us were talking about it. That's probably worth unpacking, but that's more than we will have time to do here. So, when Novo Nordisk started testing these drugs as an obesity treatment, the outcome of those trials suggested that these are the most effective weight-loss drugs ever. So, the main ingredient in Ozempic is semaglutide. It's part of a class of drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists, which basically just means they mimic a hormone that naturally occurs in your body called GLP-1. Semaglutide is in both Ozempic and Wegovy, but Wegovy is the one that's FDA-approved for weight loss. If these medications are paired with a healthy diet and exercise, people who are on semaglutide lost, on average, 15% of their body weight. The people who were just dieting and exercising lost, on average, 2.4% A newer drug made by Eli Lilly called tirzepatide did even better in its clinical trials, with people losing an average of 20% of their body weight. And so based on that data, we started to have all this very hyped news coverage about how these drugs were a game changer and a blockbuster and how maybe obesity would be cured forever, which honestly is kind of a bizarre framing. Even from the very first studies, there were people who were not responding to these drugs. Yes, it's a really big deal that 86% of people in a trial lost a significant amount of weight. However, that means 14% of people didn't. Despite all this talk about miracle drugs, the figures are basically the same for both semaglutide and tirzepatide. Roughly one in 10 people don't lose significant weight while on this medication and are what's called nonresponders. I really wanted to speak to someone who went through this, so I put a survey up on BI's social-media channels, and that's how I found Erika. It's working for other people. Why isn't it working for me and my body chemistry? I'm mad it didn't work, but then it just, I accept it, and I just got to find another way to lose the weight. Erika says her doctor didn't warn her that these drugs don't work for everybody. Like many of us, most of her information came mainly from media coverage. When you set these drugs up as a miracle or a magic pill, you're also setting people up for massive disappointment if they had high hopes of weight loss and then these drugs don't work for them. There is one more thing that a lot of coverage has missed. Real life is not the same as a clinical trial. Since those first trials and all that news coverage, there's been more data about what real-world usage looks like. A 2023 study followed people on semaglutide for 52 weeks, and those people lost an average of 4.4% of their body weight. So we went from 15% down to 4%, which is a dramatic difference. Most of the early coverage of these drugs used the numbers from the clinical trials, which makes sense because it was the first time these drugs were studied. The subsequent real-world-usage impacts have not gotten as much press coverage, and that definitely feeds into an inflated sense of how revolutionary these drugs could be. Certainly, they are a really big deal. They're more effective than prior drugs, but there are limitations. The other thing that I think might be getting lost here is that weight loss from these drugs will have a plateau, which is similar to diet, to exercise, and even to bariatric surgery. At some point, every weight-loss intervention plateaus. There's this popular conception that losing weight is the hard part and maintaining weight loss should be easy. What we know is that it's actually the opposite, right? The maintenance of weight loss is actually the hardest part. You wouldn't want a drug that allows you to lose unlimited amounts of weight. That would be dangerous, for one, and then you'd have to go off of it when you reached your goal weight, and then you would just start to climb back up again, and it would be this constant yo-yo. However, that doesn't stop people from talking about this plateau like it's some sort of betrayal of the drug or some sort of failure of this medication. All evidence points to needing to keep taking these drugs to keep benefiting from them, which is interesting because we have study data showing that most people don't keep taking them. One study looked at thousands of people with GLP-1 prescriptions and found that about half of them stopped taking it after a year, and 70% of them stopped taking it at the two-year mark. And another study found that after stopping the medication, people regained, on average, two-thirds of the weight that they'd lost. This is perhaps another big reason to dial down the hype machine on these medications. Yes, they are a big breakthrough medically, but if people don't want to be on them, then the impact of the drugs will be much lower than were predicted in the flurry of news coverage we had to begin with. A lot of people hear that this is a long-term, potentially lifelong, medication, and they see big pharma dollar signs. The cynic in all of us sort of wakes up and says, "What a win for big pharma." It's true that it is a win for big pharma. They're probably going to make a ton of money on this, and there is absolutely no denying that. I understand why people are mistrusting of pharmaceutical companies and the media coverage around them. At this point, we've seen some very irresponsible reporting. I think it's really important to be clear-eyed about the role of big pharmaceutical companies in our society. With just a quick Google, you can see that Novo Nordisk has paid fines after being accused of shady sales tactics, they've faced criticism for spending loads of money wining and dining doctors, and that they've gotten in trouble with regulators in multiple countries. More famously, Novo Nordisk, along with other drugmakers, faced massive criticism for high insulin prices. Nowadays, insulin is less profitable than it once was, but the potential profits of weight-loss drugs remain astronomical. And make no mistake, Novo Nordisk will be cashing in on these drugs and already is. At one point, the company's valuation was bigger than the entire GDP of Denmark. Understandably, some people who don't trust big pharma or simply don't have access to these drugs are turning to natural alternatives. Let's talk a little bit more about nature's Ozempic. Nature's Ozempic. You'll find people presenting berberine, peppermint tea, green tea, vitamin B12, high-fiber diets, high-protein diets, all of these things as being natural alternatives to taking Ozempic. There are certain foods that can increase the amount of GLP-1 hormone that your body makes. The part where they get it wrong is that that doesn't necessarily equate to weight loss, which appears to be the goal of many people consuming this content. The level of GLP-1 production that diets can provide is nowhere near what you can achieve with prescription medications. These interventions are leading to supraphysiological levels of GLP-1, as opposed to modest changes in your diet or some supplement that you could take. These are just orders of magnitude different, and you're not going to see anywhere near the same effects. But between influencer nutritionists and supplement grifters, we're seeing tremendous amounts of misinformation online about how effective a GLP-1-boosting diet can be. These foods and vitamins are generally less risky than a serious prescription drug, but they're almost definitely less effective as well. This is another subject of intensive news coverage where I think we just need to turn the hype dial down a little bit and look at what the research actually tells us. I also think people pay a lot of attention to side effects of these drugs because we've had plenty of examples of prescription drugs coming onto the market and a side effect no one knew about ends up being very serious, particularly for weight-loss drugs. The most common side effects of these medications are gastrointestinal, things like nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. These can seem a little bit trivial, just like tummy trouble or whatever, but they can be quite serious. Extended periods of vomiting or diarrhea can leave you dangerously dehydrated. It's even been reported that one woman died while taking these drugs after months of gastrointestinal issues, including severe vomiting and abdominal pain. Besides the GI issues, the FDA label for these drugs includes a number of other warnings, some of which are for very serious conditions. So if we just pull up the label now, there is what's called a black-box warning about the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. The warning label mentions findings in rodents, but a GLP-1 researcher I spoke to said that the thyroid in rodents and humans is quite different. So those findings probably aren't relevant. Sometimes by putting a warning label on because of initial good intentions, you can cause more harm by scaring away people who otherwise might be willing to take this medicine and benefit from the medicine. While the link between GLP-1 medication and thyroid cancer has been hard to establish, the link between obesity and thyroid cancer is much clearer. One study found that for every five-point increase in BMI, the risk of thyroid cancer increases by 30%. There's also another category on this label called warnings and precautions, and it includes acute pancreatitis, acute gallbladder disease, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, hypersensitivity reactions, diabetic retinopathy, heart-rate increase, and suicidal behavior and ideation. The label here just says: "Monitor for depression or suicidal thoughts. Discontinue Wegovy if symptoms develop." That's not very reassuring to me. This is an ongoing and evolving thing, but the weight of evidence so far suggests that these drugs alone are not going to cause you to have suicidal thoughts. It is not uncommon for drugs to have very intimidating, if not downright scary-looking, FDA warning labels. It's important to remember that things listed on these labels are potential risks rather than guaranteed results, which actually does seem to get lost in the shuffle a bit on social media. Most of the more serious side effects of GLP-1 drugs are on the rare side. Most people who take these medications will not get pancreatitis. Sometimes people wonder why a drug could be approved if it has so many alarming side effects, but it's really not uncommon. If you look at metformin, a very popular diabetes medication, it has a warning for potentially fatal lactic acidosis. If you look at the label for ibuprofen, it has a warning about potential increased risk of stroke. These things are calculated in the context of being sick. If you take these drugs and don't have a medical need for them, your risk calculation is different and you are putting yourself at greater risk of harm. Your neighbor who is interested in taking this medicine to lose 10 pounds so they can get into a size-eight dress for Uncle Harry's wedding, they weren't studied in a clinical trial. But besides what's on the label, which is scary enough on its own, there's all these rumors on social media about a whole other category of effects that are mostly cosmetic, things like "Ozempic face" or hair loss. And it's not just hair loss. There's been a ton of concern about how much muscle people lose while taking GLP-1 drugs. However, whenever you lose weight, even if it's just through diet and exercise, you do tend to lose some lean muscle. One thing that's often forgotten in this whole conversation is that weight loss itself can have some very serious side effects, particularly rapid or extreme weight loss. Even losing weight fast through diet has been linked to hair loss, muscle loss, depression, gallstones -- all side effects that overlap with the side effects of Ozempic. So it's really hard to tell where one ends and the other begins. Personally, I think this is just another example of how the conversation around Ozempic has just gotten really weird. People seem to want there to be a punishment for taking a vanity drug and almost gleefully report this idea that your face or your hair or whatever would fail you when you've taken a step to make your body look nicer. At least, that's the perception. And to be sure, some people have taken Ozempic as a vanity drug. These drugs became a household name because celebrities were touting them for weight loss, and in many cases, already-thin celebrities were touting their weight-loss benefits. So, we've talked about the bad, but there are also some really interesting positive effects that these drugs potentially have. Not only do they make you crave less food, they make you desire different, usually healthier food. There's a physiological response that causes some people to be more preoccupied with food than others. People I talk to who have been suffering from food noise say the drug feels like a switch is being flipped in their brains. People have now reported other cravings going away too, like the urge to online shop. These drugs could help with all kinds of conditions -- Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, alcohol addiction, and other types of addiction, depression. There's even anecdotal reports of Ozempic babies, which are people whose fertility improved while they were on these drugs. All these things aren't so much side effects as they are potentially brand-new indications for the drugs, brand-new conditions that they could treat. GLP-1 drugs have a really unusually high number of potential new indications. About one in eight Americans have already tried GLP-1 medications, and this explosion of interest has led to something we've never quite seen before. One of the strangest elements of this rush for everyone to try semaglutide is that it put the drug in shortage. And when drugs are on the official FDA shortage list, compounding pharmacies can make their own versions. Compounded versions of these drugs are not FDA-approved or -reviewed, and because these pharmacies are regulated at the state level, there's no data available for how many people are taking compounded GLP-1s. In an environment this confusing, it becomes easier to take advantage of people. I spoke to a researcher who purposefully ordered compounded semaglutide from shady online sellers just to see what he would get. We looked at the online pharmacies that were no prescription and were highest ranked in search results. So these were some of the websites that consumers will see first. Of the six drugs that he ordered, three never came at all. They were total scams. So they took the three prescriptions that they actually received and put the drugs to the test, and what they found was evidence of contamination and improper amounts of the active ingredient, semaglutide. The FDA has also issued a warning about some compounders using semaglutide salt, which is generally used only for research and is not approved for use in humans. So, for consumers, the most important thing is to understand that when you source it from a no-prescription online pharmacy, there's a lot of risks. Either fraud, incorrect product, or, again, you're not getting a product that is medically necessary for you or appropriate for you. Offering no-prescription versions of prescription drugs is illegal, but there's also what feels like a tidal wave of buzzy online health startups who can temporarily sell totally legally. I actually went through the process of being prescribed compounded semaglutide. I went through an online pharmacy where all I had to do was fill out a survey and then do a video telehealth visit with a doctor to be prescribed these drugs. I went through this process for reporting purposes to see how easy it would be to get these drugs, and it turns out it was pretty easy, which, depending how much you value drug regulation, could be kind of concerning. There was sort of no question that I was going to get these drugs. From the second the call started, it was a given. I don't know why, but I thought he might challenge me and say, like, "Ah, these are some pretty heavy-duty side effects. Are you sure you want to take these drugs to lose a small amount of weight?" But he didn't. And the doctor that I spoke to in that process did not give any indication that I would need to stay on these drugs to maintain the weight loss. I'm not saying all this to fearmonger about compounding pharmacies, but it is kind of wild how little we know about how many people are taking drugs from compounding pharmacies when we do know that they come with a higher degree of risk. However, there is one considerable upside, and that's that for some people, compounding pharmacies offer a cheaper version of these drugs. In my case, a month's supply of semaglutide cost $250. The list price for Ozempic in the United States is almost $1,000 for a month's supply. For Wegovy, it's $1,349. Those are shocking price tags. You can find economists estimating that GLP-1 medications will add $1 trillion in healthcare spending to the US. Then we have other economists estimating that it's actually somewhere between 20% and 50% of that. And it's not really possible to know who's right or wrong because the actual prices paid to drugmakers are secret. And that's one of the many oddities of the American healthcare system, is that no one knows exactly what drugmakers actually make from selling their drugs. It's considered proprietary information. At the end of the day, a lot of people seem to want it to be true that these drugs could actually save healthcare systems money, that we spend so much on treating obesity and related conditions that these drugs could actually be a net money saver. And while that might eventually happen, especially if the cost of these drugs goes down, that is a very rare feat for a drug to pull off. The most important thing to remember is that if you see estimates of how much a certain drug is going to cost US healthcare systems or how much obesity costs America in general, remember that these are really rough estimates. And that's important because the stigma that people with obesity face is often couched in this idea that they're a tremendous financial burden to the healthcare system. I have seen countless comments saying, "Why do you need Ozempic if you can just eat healthier?" "Why do you need to take these drugs?" "What you're looking for is willpower." It simply doesn't make sense to talk about Ozempic as being the easy way out. The easy way out implies there's another way out, and for a lot of people, there just isn't. What these medicines have taught us is that a huge number of people living with obesity, they were restricting their calories, they were following diets, they were exercising, and it just didn't work for them even though they really wanted it to work. And now we have something that helps them, and guess what? They're losing weight. We've been lied to about weight loss for a long time, and we're only just starting to figure it out. The reality is that we, both as a culture and the medical community, have been significantly underplaying how difficult it is to lose weight and especially how difficult it is to maintain weight loss. We have a ton of data on this at this point, and we know that drastic weight loss is exceedingly rare and is usually temporary. Over time, we've also learned that exercise is not nearly as big of a factor in weight loss as people tend to suggest. It has many benefits and is still important for overall health, but burning more calories is not a guaranteed path to weight loss. Many studies have shown at this point that even in the best of circumstances, where we're combining diet, exercise, and behavioral counseling, people tend to only lose 5% to 10% of their body weight. Then, after that, your body fights back. When you lose weight, your body starts to release hormones that increase appetite and reduce feelings of fullness. So there's actually a biological mechanism encouraging people to eat more as weight is lost. Studies on people who've lost quite a lot of weight have found that they burn fewer calories than scientists expected, even when you account for the fact that their bodies are smaller and they're carrying less weight around. If you lose roughly 20 pounds or so and you're maintaining that 20-pound weight loss, you're probably burning about 250 calories per day less than you were before you lost the weight. And we've known that for a very long time. The advice that doctors gave for years was that all it takes is small tweaks to your lifestyle. Swap your bag of chips for an apple or take the stairs. You can still find all kinds of advice like that online. And it's actually, frankly, bizarre that after decades of research supporting the idea that this is a very complex issue, so many people insist on acting like it's easy. It is understandable to have anxiety about medicating millions of people for what's seen as a wider societal issue. And some people say this is a Band-Aid on a bigger problem, those bigger problems being things like our food system or our sedentary lifestyles. And, yes, there would likely be tremendous social benefit to addressing those very complex systemic problems, but for now, we have a relatively safe and effective drug that can give people another tool to manage their health in the meantime. - Top 5 GLP-1 Side Effects and How to Fix Them | Doctor Explains: Kind: captions Language: en The GLP-1 medicines are amazing, but they do have side effects. So, today I want to go over the top five side effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists and what to do about them. I'm Dr. Spencer Nadulski, a triple board certified obesity specialist physician, and I've overseen thousands of patients myself and overseen tens of thousands if you include the doctors that have been under me at the various programs I've worked at. I'm going to go over the side effects in terms of what the trials see and what also we see in clinical practice and what we do about them. Number one, by far the most common side effect you're going to see is nausea. If you've taken one of these medicines, you've probably had at least a mild to moderate amount of nausea, some people don't have any nausea, which is lucky for them. While some people unfortunately are unlucky and have a moderate to severe amount of nausea with some vomiting involved. When you look at the trial data though, most of the nausea is at the beginning of the trial. It spikes up and then over time it starts to subside. And this is what we see in clinical practice. Most of the time once people are to their maintenance dose, they have mild to no nausea at all. The goal is to prevent the nausea in the first place. Luckily, I have a team of amazing dieticians who help my patients through dietary means to help minimize and avoid nausea in the first place. Me as the medical doctor, I want to make sure I only titrate up the medicine once the nausea is mostly resolved. It doesn't have to be completely resolved. Sometimes it takes a lot longer, but ideally you're not going up in your dose of the medicine until you're like around a two out of five of nausea severity. For example, if you're on 0.25 milligs of Wikovi and you're feeling like you're going to throw up and the next month you ask your doctor for a refill and the doctor tries to put you up to.5 millig, I would probably hold off on that. Same thing with turbatiz. Say you're on 2.5 millig and you're feeling a lot of nausea. I would make sure that you're not going up to that 5 millig unless that nausea is very mild. To help prevent the nausea in the first place from a nutritional standpoint, the biggest things are very heavy fatty foods. So some of this stuff is pretty common sense when you're trying to lose weight, but think of things like pizza, wings, chips, French fries, burgers, those types of things. Very heavy, very fatty meals. A lot of times patients learn this because they ate one of these fatty meals in the beginning and they felt terrible the next day. This doesn't mean you can't enjoy those foods once in a while later on in your journey. And you can even try to enjoy them early on, but just know that if you try to eat a highfat meal like pizza, chips, wings, whatever, you may feel pretty terrible the next day. You may even feel it within hours of eating that food. The mechanism of the nausea is kind of interesting. Most people think of it as the slowing of your gastric emptying. That may be related. However, there's actually areas in the brain that relate to where the medicines hit for satiety and help you not eat so much and help with the food noise and all that. And then there's other areas of the brain that actually are related to the nausea. And fun tidbit, researchers and scientists right now are trying to make a more targeted GLP-1 receptor agonist that only hits those parts of the brain that help with satiety and food noise while not hitting those parts of the brain that cause nausea. We'll see if they make any progress there. uh it might be a long time before they get there. Another dietary tip is that if you're eating already a lower fat type of diet and you're like, gosh, I'm still feeling nauseous, sometimes breaking up those larger meals and making them a little bit smaller. So instead of three larger meals per day, it might be four to five or even six smaller meals per day. Again, I'm lucky that I have dietitians who will work with the patient on an individual basis and strategize with them in their own life. The other thing I do from a medical standpoint is if they're on let's say wiggoi some magide and they're having a lot of nausea despite all the dietary efforts that we put in to help minimize that nausea. Sometimes I will switch them to tzepite or zepbound. The gip components a gp1/gip co-ceptor agonist that gip component actually works up in the brain and has anti-imetic properties which is kind of interesting whereas the GLP-1 receptor agonist only and simaglletide doesn't have that property. patients tend to tolerate that turepide much better. So, we'll switch them over if insurance allows for it or if they want to pay out of pocket if insurance doesn't cover it. And lastly, I try to avoid this, but I will do it for my patients if I need to. I can use anti-nausea medicines. My go-to is Zopran or Andatrron. I use the oral dissolving tablet on the tongue. Some people like to do the swallow tablet. It's up to them. Once in a while, Zopran doesn't work or the undancatron doesn't work. And once in a while I do use reglin or metylopramide. This is a motility drug and sometimes this helps a little bit better than the zopran. I try not to do that very often. It's only in refractory cases where the zopran is not really helping. Make sure you talk to your doctor before you take any of these types of drugs or even think about it. Obviously, they need to prescribe it, but don't be taking your friend's drugs. Okay. Second most common thing we see, constipation. Now instead of nausea where it's a spike in the beginning and it starts uh lessening throughout your GLP-1 receptor agonist journey, constipation tends to be constant. So in order to prevent this in the first place, we're going to do some dietary strategies. Again, lucky I have amazing dietitians who help with this. We have resources to make sure we prevent this in our patients in the first place. But here are my general tips. Number one, of course, you're going to want to drink a lot of fluids. You know, some people just completely forget to eat and then they don't even drink fluid. So, make sure you're staying hydrated. You don't have to hit some number of uh cups per day of water. Everybody always says drink eight cups of water per day, but like honestly, just try to keep your urine a very light yellow to clear. Number two, try to eat whole food fibrous types of foods. Don't avoid carbohydrates because you think they're going to cause you to gain weight. They're not going to be their calorie content. They contain fiber unless you're eating highly processed carbohydrate containing foods. So try to eat whole, unprocessed types of carbohydrate containing foods, lentils, beans, fruits, vegetables, those types of things. Again, this stuff is common sense. Obviously, if you're trying to lose weight, those things are good for you anyway, but try to focus on these types of foods to avoid the constipation from happening in the first place. The other thing I do is obviously for weight loss purposes, we want to keep people moving, but physical activity with the fluid and high fibrous foods can help keeping your bowels moving. The next thing we do is supplement with fiber if we need to if we feel like they can't get enough in their diet. We start with psyllium husk, although too much psyllium husk can make the constipation worse in some individuals. So, we want to make sure we're talking to the patient, asking what their stools are like and their bowel movements. We may need to switch the fiber supplementation, switch it to some other uh type of fiber. Then lastly, we may actually start looking at laxatives for helping them move their bowels. My general go-to for uh the laxatives is Murax or polyethylene glycol. Really easy to add to whatever kind of drinks, flavored drinks that you want. It goes down pretty easily. Just a serving a day. Again, you want to talk to your provider, make sure that it's not interfering with anything like that before going to that route. But Murax or polyethylene glycol is one thing that I do. The third thing we see a lot of is reflux. So because the medicines slow down your gastric emptying, the food contents can stay in your stomach longer which then give it a more of a chance to reflux up into your esophagus and then you start feeling that reflux. The same thing for reflux is like for the constipation and nausea where dietary and lifestyle modifications can help a lot. This is where I love my dietitians again of course. However, easy things like making sure we're sitting up after meals. Sometimes we have to lower the bulk in our meals, smaller meals if we need to do that so that the food goes down a little bit faster or there's less bulk sitting in your stomach. Always talk to your doctor before starting any over-the-counter medicines regardless if they're supplements or medicines. The fourth thing we see is once in a while people start developing diarrhea which kind of goes against the idea of gastric slowing because we see with the constipation you know it makes sense if things are slowing down things aren't moving through your bowels as quickly but with diarrhea things are moving very quickly. Other neurobiologists I've talked to said maybe the medicine hits in certain places of the brain that are similar to like chemotherapy or other drugs that cause fatigue. That's kind of a side effect. - Understanding GLP-1 Medications: Kind: captions Language: en Have type 2 diabetes? You may be wondering what you can do to be as healthy as possible. Fortunately, there are many things you can do to manage your blood sugar. With type 2 diabetes, your levels of a vital hormone that aids food digestion and metabolism are lower than normal. When that hormone is low, it's hard for your body to balance your blood sugar. GLP-1 receptor agonist, also known as GLP-1RAs, are medications that boost that hormone to do four important things. Help your body release insulin when needed. Keep your liver from releasing too much sugar into your bloodstream. Help slow food leaving your stomach, reducing blood sugar spikes. Help your brain tell your body when you're full. All four actions benefit you by reducing appetite, lowering your A1C levels, lowering risk of certain heart problems if you already have heart disease or are at high risk, helping slow kidney problems if you've developed certain complications. GLP-1RA medications are available as daily or once-weekly injectable devices or a pill. Tell your provider if you have a personal or family history of thyroid cancer, pancreatitis, gallbladder problems. If so, you should avoid GLP-1RA medications. Common side effects with these medications include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation. The dose of GLP-1RA medications is increased slowly over time to decrease side effects. Side effects usually subside and may stop after a few weeks. Here are some ways you can help minimize side effects. Eat more frequently with smaller, less fatty meals. Eat slowly. Stop eating at first signs of fullness. Don't lie down after eating. GLP-1RA medications alone do not cause your blood sugar to go too low. However, if you also take insulin or certain oral diabetes medications, you need to watch for low blood sugar. When you have type 2 diabetes, you might require more or different medications over time. Research shows that using medications like GLP-1RAs early in the course of diabetes can have lasting positive effects. GLP-1RA medications correct many problems caused by type 2 diabetes, so they can help you reach your diabetes management goals. Ask your healthcare provider and diabetes care and education specialist if these medications fit into your treatment plan and are covered by your insurance. For more information, please visit diabeteseducator.org/glp1.
