- GLP-1 Receptor Agonists | Incretin Therapies for Type 2 Diabetes | Management of Diabetes Mellitus: Kind: captions Language: en The GLP-1 receptor agonists are a category of medications known as the incrretins. Normally when glucose is given orally it triggers a greater insulin release than when the same amount of glucose is given IV. This phenomenon called the incrretin effect highlights the role of glucose sensitive receptors in the gastrointestinal tract. These receptors stimulate the release of hormones such as glucagon like peptide also known as GLP-1. Unfortunately, in type 2 diabetes, the incrretin effect is diminished by mimicking the action of natural GLP-1. The GLP-1 agonists enhance insulin release in response to food, helping lower blood sugar levels effectively. GLP-1 is released by cells in the small intestine after a meal. Once in circulation, it travels to the pancreas and stimulates insulin secretion while also suppressing glucagon release. It slows gastric emptying which increases satiety and helps patients feel full sooner and eat less. This delay in digestion also slows the postmeal rise in blood sugar. Together, these effects improve blood sugar control and support weight loss. For patients with type 2 diabetes, where the natural GLP-1 response is reduced, GLP-1 receptor agonists provide a valuable way to restore these benefits. A newer addition to this class combines GLP-1 receptor agonist with another hormone called gastric inhibitory polyeptide or GIP. GIP works similarly to GLP-1 by enhancing insulin release in response to food. This combination found in the medication tepatide offers impressive efficacy for lowering blood sugar, enhancing satiety, and promoting weight loss. Unlike traditional GLP-1 receptor agonists, GIP does not slow gastric emptying, which may help reduce some of the gastrointestinal side effects commonly associated with this class of medications. Beyond their role in lowering blood sugars, several GLP-1 receptor agonists have cardiovascular benefits and should be the initial treatment options for patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease. While the combination GLP-1 GIP receptor agonists haven't yet demonstrated similar benefits, they are considered safe from a cardiovascular outcomes perspective. Several GLP-1 receptor agonists have shown potential to slow the progression of diabetic kidney disease in patients with chronic kidney disease, offering an additional layer of protection. While they may help reduce the risk of worsening kidney function, they do not reverse existing damage. Emerging evidence also suggests that combination therapies like trespatide may help preserve kidney function compared to glargene, though long-term studies are still ongoing to confirm these benefits. The GLP-1 receptor agonists have very high efficacy in lowering blood sugars and are also a reasonable option for patients with type 2 diabetes without other complications to help lower A1C and achieve glucose control. On average, they can reduce A1C by about 1% and the combination therapies can achieve reductions of up to 2%. Most of these medications are injectables, but they are convenient to use with many available as once weekly injections. This dosing schedule can help improve adherence, especially for patients who find daily medications challenging. Like any treatment, GLP-1 receptor agonists have potential side effects. The most common is nausea, which occurs due to the slowing of gastric emptying. The severity of nausea varies widely. Some patients tolerate these medications well while others may struggle even at low doses. Gradual dose titration can help minimize this side effect. These medications are contraindicated in gastroparesis as their effects on gastric emptying could worsen symptoms. There are other considerations as well. Pancreatitis has been reported in some patients using GLP-1 receptor agonist, though it's unclear if the medications are the direct cause. If pancreatitis develops, it's appropriate to stop the medication. Pre-clinical animal studies did show an increase in sea cell hyperplasia, which could increase the risk of meillary thyroid cancer, a cancer of the CE cells in the thyroid. It is unclear if this is relevant for humans. As a precaution, these medications are not recommended for individuals with a personal or family history of meillary thyroid cancer or multiple endocrine neoplasia types one or two. However, there is no increased risk for other types of thyroid cancer. One major advantage of GLP1 and GIP receptor agonists is their low risk of hypoglycemia. Since they only enhance insulin release when blood sugar levels are elevated, such as after a meal, they are a safe option for patients at risk of low blood sugar. Additionally, their weight loss benefits have led to their approval as a weight loss treatment even for individuals without diabetes. For patients with type 2 diabetes who are also working on weight management, these medications can be particularly helpful. So, I hope you like this [music] video. Absolutely. - Branded vs. Compounded GLP-1s: What’s the Difference? | GoodRx: Kind: captions Language: en-US - When we use the term GLP-1 medications, we’re talking about brand-name medications like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Saxenda, Zepbound, Trulicity, and Victoza. Some are approved for Type 2 diabetes, others are approved for weight management, and then some of them even have additional health conditions they’re approved for like obstructive sleep apnea or to improve cardiovascular health. (gentle acoustic guitar music) Compounded GLP-1s are specially made versions. They contain the same active ingredient, but they’re not exactly the same as the manufactured medication, and they’ve been allowed because the manufactured versions were in shortage. Now, that being said, the tirzepatide shortage ended in late 2024, and the semaglutide shortage ended in early 2025, so most of these compounded versions are no longer allowed per the FDA. Branded GLP-1 medications have gone through a rigorous amount of research and testing to make sure that they’re safe and effective and there’s very clear dosage administration guidelines for the health conditions they’re approved for. Compounded medications are made to order. They’re not exactly the same as the FDA-approved version, so they have more inherent risks when it comes to their safety as well as their effectiveness. There’s a few different things that can differ. It could be the dose, the dosage form, which is how it’s administered, and the different ingredients inside of the medication itself. can sometimes be more expensive than traditional manufactured medications, but sometimes they can be less expensive depending on the dosage form and the medication involved. When it comes to concerns about cost when you’re switching from a compounded version to the brand-name version or the manufactured version, I’d say there’s two main things to consider. The first is you get what you pay for, so cheaper isn’t always safer or better. The second is that there are a lot of additional steps you can take to actually save on the FDA-approved versions, and those steps aren’t available for the compounded versions. (music fades)

So additional muscle loss can lead to weakness, difficulty walking, loss of independence, higher risk of disability, nursing home admission, and even increased mortality. There's also bone loss known as osteoporosis. Losing weight quickly in any way can reduce bone density. Less bone and less muscle equals major fall in fracture risk. One long-term study showed weight loss increased fracture risk by 39%. Third, dehydration and falls. Common GLP-1 side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. For older adults, these can be more severe thanks to age related changes in the gut. Dehydration leads to dizziness, fainting, and falls. One of the leading causes of injury in seniors. Number four, kidney function risks. Dehydration can strain the kidneys and contribute to acute kidney injury, especially in adults who already have kidney issues. Fifth on the list, drug interactions, which is known as polyfarm pharmacy. Older adults often take multiple medications because GLP wants slow digestion. Other medications may stay in the body longer or GI side effects can worsen. And finally, frailty and unintended weight loss. Doctors emphasize that in adults over 65, weight loss itself can increase mortality, especially if someone unintentionally loses more than 10% of their body weight. So for seniors, the goal isn't get the scale lower. It's preserve strength, mobility, and independence. Let's talk about what the experts are recommending. Doctors like Dr. Gant and Dr. John Batsis agree on one thing. GLP1s can help older adults, but only with careful management. You want to start low and go slow. The number one rule in geriatric medicine. Older adults often need lower starting doses, slower dose increases, and longer time between dose changes. This dramatically reduces GI side effects and dehydration risk. You also want to prioritize muscle and bone protection. Strength preserves independence, period. Essential strategies for this would be resistance training at least two times per week with 8 to 12 reps per exercise and five to seven exercises. Include your legs, arms, core, and upper body. And you want to add weight or resistance bands as tolerated. Example exercises that doctors and physical therapists are recommending are sit to stand, squats, planks, heel raises, chair yoga, pilates, water aerobics, and light weight lifting. Protein intake is non-negotiable. Older adults need more protein than younger people, about 1 to 1.2 g per kilogram of body weight daily. Examples would be a palmsized portion of chicken, fish, and tofu. You want to also eat nuts, seeds, and Greek yogurt to get that protein. And make sure you're getting protein at every meal and snack. You want to make sure that you're monitoring closely. Older adults on GLP1s should have regular checkups of kidney function, hydration status, muscle strength, gate and mobility, bone density if you're at risk, overall frailty, and medication interactions. And finally, you do want to coordinate with your doctor. This includes reviewing all medications, deciding if weight loss is appropriate for you, setting realistic goals, function over the number on the scale. Many older adults care most about being able to get up from a chair, walk independently, play with their grandchildren, and avoid nursing home placement. GLP1s should support these goals, not undermine them. So, what is the future of GLP1s in older adults? Even though the data in seniors is limited, especially over age 75, doctors are becoming more optimistic. But the big unanswered questions remain. Are the improvements due to the drug itself or simply because people lose weight, they move more, and they reduce their inflammation? Do these drugs directly or indirectly reduce cancer or dementia risk? Researchers are actively studying this right now. GLP-1 medications can be safe and effective for older adults, but only with the right plan. The benefits are better blood sugar, reduced inflammation, improved heart health, and potential protection against some diseases. First, let's define what overweight and obesity really mean as a medical condition. These conditions refer to excessive or abnormal fat accumulation that poses a risk to someone's health. Historically, determining if a person had overweight or obesity came down to calculating their body mass index. Their body mass index or BMI is simply a ratio between their height and their weight. A BMI that calculated out to 25 to 29.9 would be categorized as overweight. A BMI of 30 to 34.9 would be classified as obesity class one. 35 to 39.9 is obesity class 2. And anything above 40 is considered obesity class three. Sometimes I hear people referring to their BMI and their body fat percentage interchangeably, but that is not quite accurate. BMI does not specifically address body fat percentage. It's just height and weight. Body fat percentage gives us an idea of of someone's body weight. What percentage is fat? And what percentage of that weight comes from lean tissue? That's muscle, bone, water, things on our body that are not specifically atapost tissue. And this is important because what we have found is there are some folks in the overweight, maybe even in the obese BMI categories, that their weight is actually made up of a higher amount of muscle. And those folks are actually more metabolically healthy traditionally than folks who have a similar BMI but more of their body weight is atapost tissue or fat tissue instead of muscle. In fact, at the end of 2024, the American Medical Association proposed a new criteria for defining obesity, which would include yes, calculating BMI because it is easy, accessible, and inexpensive to do, but then also for folks who have an elevated BMI calculation, digging a little bit deeper into a body fat percentage or where the atapost tissue is stored on the body because even that can impact someone's relative risk of developing a chronic disease. For instance, if someone has more atipose tissue in their midsection, that is more dangerous when it comes to developing things like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, cancer, etc. Whereas, if a person stores more of their body weight in their butt, their thighs, their extremities, that is actually a little bit more protective from some of our chronic diseases. GLP1 dosing is an off label strategy, meaning it is not FDA approved and not part of standard prescribing guidelines. It's generally used after a patient reaches a healthy weight, during a maintenance phase, not active weight loss, and only under medical supervision. GLP-1 medications are designed for once weekly dosing to maintain stable therapeutic levels. So changing that schedule is a clinical judgment call not a universal recommendation. GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and herzepatide have a halflife of about 5 days. That means by day seven the standard dosing interval drug levels are already declining. The study reviewed medical records from 30 patients who had reached a normal weight or resolved weight related conditions. After all this growth, is any of it actually working at a national level? New data this week says it might be. New data from Epic Research shows just how fast GLP1 use has expanded in the United States over the last 5 years. It also suggests obesity rates may be finally starting to move downward at a population level. According to Epic Research, GLP-1 prescription rates among US adults rose from 1888 prescriptions per 100,000 patients in the second quarter of 2021 to 8,819 per 100,000 by the first quarter of 2026. That is more than a 400% increase in just 5 years. The data comes from Cosmos, a large healthcare database built through Epic Systems. Cosmos includes deidentified electronic health record data from more than 304 million patient records across 2,000 hospitals and more than 47,000 clinics. That scale matters because it shows what is happening in realworld medical practice across the country, not just inside controlled clinical trials. The database lets researchers track prescribing trends, BMI changes, diagnosis, and treatment patterns across millions of patients over time. Now, these are observational studies, so they can identify trends and associations, but cannot fully prove cause and effect. The report shows simaglutide and trazepatide drove most of the increase in prescribing. Back in 2021, simaglutide accounted for roughly 680 prescriptions per 100,000 patients, while doolaglutide was the most commonly prescribed GLP-1 and about 790 prescriptions per 100,000. By the first quarter of 2026, transepide had become the most prescribed GLP-1 in the data set at roughly 4,700 prescriptions per 100,000 patients. Some ofide climbed sharply too to around 3,900 per 100,000. Use of older GLP-1 medications declined as newer treatments replace them. Epic research also tracked changes in BMI across the adult population during the same period. According to the report, the share of US adults classified as obese fell from 42% in the second quarter of 2021 to 40.7% in the first quarter of 2026. The decline was gradual with most of the movement coming in the later part of the study period. The share of adults in the healthy weight category rose slightly from 25.1% to 25.6%. The report does not claim GLP-1 medications alone cause the shift. Population level obesity trends are shaped by many factors including health care access, socioeconomic conditions, lifestyle changes, demographics, and which patients are actually able to get the treatment. But the timing is hard to ignore. Simaglutide received FDA approval for chronic weight management in 2021, followed by Trespatide in 2023. Our next few stories look at what these medications are doing inside the body. Starting with one that anyone in maintenance will recognize. Why does the weight loss eventually slow down? Researchers at the National Institutes of Health released new findings this week that may help explain why some patients respond differently to treatment and why weight loss so often slows down over time. The study was conducted by researchers at the NIH's National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences. It focused on what happens inside brain cells after simaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors. Scientists already know GLP-1 medications affect appetite related regions of the brain. The study looked more closely at the signaling happening inside neurons after the medication binds to those receptors. Using fluorescent imaging in living mouse brain tissue, researchers examined simaglutide's effect in the area postrema, a region involved in appetite and feeding behavior. They focused on a signaling molecule called CM which helps carry signals inside cells after GLP-1 receptors are activated. According to the NIS researchers, simaglutide increased CM and C activity inside neurons, but the response varied significantly from cell to cell. Some neurons held elevated C levels for longer periods, while others showed only a temporary bump before the signaling faded. Michael Crashes, Ph.D., a senior investigator at NIDK and co-author of the study, said it was not an all or nothing phenomenon. We observed that CM responses across cells varied on a continuum. Researchers believe some neurons may reduce or internalize their GLP-1 receptors over time, which could weakening signaling and help explain the weight loss plateaus many patients hit during long-term treatment. The team also tested whether they could stretch the signaling response out. Using rooflast, a drug that blocks the PDE4 enzyme responsible for breaking down CM. They were able to shift more neur more neurons toward a sustained response. Andrew Lutus, PhD, an investigator at NIDK and co-author of the study, said, "We know much less about the nuts and bolts of what goes on within the neurons that these medications target. By digging into these mechanisms, we're beginning to answer some of these questions." The researchers said the findings may help explain why patients respond differently to GLP-1 medications and why treatment effects can eventually plateau. Keep in mind this was done in mice in brain tissue observed over several hours, not long-term treatment in humans. Researchers said future studies will look at these signaling effects over longer stretches of time. The findings were published by the NIH as researchers continue studying how GLP-1 medications affect appetite behavior and weight regulation at the cellular level. It's a lot of data. This next one is about hormones and it's getting attention from a field you might not expect, urology. New research presented at the American Urological Association meeting adds to growing evidence that GLP1s may improve testosterone levels in some men with obesity and type 2 diabetes. These drugs, as we all know, are mainly prescribed for obesity and diabetes, but researchers are increasingly studying how the weight loss and metabolic improvements that come with them may affect hormone health, sexual health, and reproductive function in men. The research discussed at the meeting looked at men with obesity and type 2 diabetes treated with GLP-1s, including semaglutide, dulaglutide, and tzepide. According to researchers, testosterone levels improved significantly during treatment. One retrospective analysis of 110 men found that after 18 months of GLP-1 treatment, the share of men with testosterone in the normal range rose from 53% to 77%. Average body weight dropped by roughly 10% over the same period, while total testosterone rose by 18%. The study excluded men already using testosterone replacement therapy or other hormone treatments, which let researchers focus specifically on changes tied to GLP-1 treatment and weight loss. Researchers and physicians say the findings line up with what obesity medicine has shown for years. Substantial weight loss often improves testosterone levels in men with obesity. A 2025 systematic review and meta analysis also found GLP-1 receptor agonists were associated with increased bioavailable testosterone and better blood sugar control in men. Researchers noted that obesity itself is strongly linked to lower testosterone. Excess body fat, especially visceral fat around the internal organs, can disrupt hormone regulation and reduce testosterone production. Healthline quoted endocrinologist Beverly Chang, who we've interviewed here of Wild Cornell Medicine, who said, "The findings track with what we would expect based on how weight loss affects testosterone concentrations." Researchers emphasize that the medications themselves may not directly drive testosterone production. The improvement may come largely from weight loss reduced visceral fat, better insulin sensitivity, and the broader metabolic gains that come with GLP-1 treatment. This is also part of how much wider GLP-1 research has gotten. Early studies focused mostly on blood sugar and weight loss. Newer work is now digging into cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, sleep apnea, addiction pathways, fertility, hormone regulation, and inflammatory conditions. Researchers caution that more long-term data is still needed. Much of the current evidence comes from retrospective analysis, observational studies, or smaller data sets, not large randomized trials built specifically to study testosterone. The findings presented at the meeting have not yet been fully published in a peer-reviewed journal. Your biology is ancient. Your environment is new. And this conflict makes weight loss feel like swimming against a biochemical current. But it gets more interesting once you understand the wiring. In the deepest part of your brain lies the hypothalamus, the lizard brain, responsible for survival, temperature, thirst, stress, and hunger. This region defends your body fat set point with military precision. It uses two hormones to do it. Grein, which is essentially the gas pedal, is produced by the stomach when empty. It travels up the vagus nerve and says we need food. This is primal overpowering and has been shown in nature reviews endocrinology to override willpower completely. If you inject sugar into someone's bloodstream, the insulin response is small. But if they drink the same sugar, the insulin response is huge. Why? Because the gut warns the body in advance. Intestinal cells called L cells release a hormone called GLP-1. GLP1 does three things immediately. It prepares the pancreas for insulin. It slows the stomach. It tells the brain we're satisfied. If scientists wanted to use GLP-1 as a drug, they needed to outsmart DPP4. The breakthrough came from a creature most people have never even heard of, the Gilla Monster.   3. @TheAlchemistZero1: The Cult of Certainty: How Scientism Mistakes Symbols for Reality

Abstract

This essay dismantles the illusion of scientific and mathematical authority over reality. It argues that physics, mathematics, and cosmology have become modern priesthoods—fluent in symbols, blind to their own assumptions, and convinced that their linguistic constructions constitute the world itself. Beneath their precision lies an unacknowledged act of faith: the belief that their frameworks, born of human limitation, can speak for the infinite complexity of Nature.

1. Introduction: The Rise of a New Dogma

Where religion once claimed the cosmos, scientism now reigns. Its prophets wear lab coats instead of robes, its scriptures are peer-reviewed, and its miracles are equations. It promises salvation through measurement, yet forgets that every instrument was built by fallible hands, every metric chosen by fallible minds.

Science is not the problem; its humility is. Scientism—the conviction that empirical method alone exhausts reality—is philosophy dressed in the armor of precision, mistaking its own reflection for the world.

2. The Frame That Sees Only Itself

Every experiment begins with a premise: what to measure, how to measure, what counts as real. Instruments do not reveal Nature; they negotiate with it, returning answers framed by the questions we taught them to ask.

To believe otherwise is to mistake a telescope for the stars. The data that scientists prize as “objective” already arrive pre-filtered through design, expectation, and interpretation. What emerges as “fact” is not a message from Nature but a conversation among humans—mediated by language, technology, and theory.

Scientism hides this circularity behind jargon and precision. Its practitioners forget that a system cannot justify its own axioms; the framework that defines observation cannot step outside itself to claim omniscience.

3. Mathematics: The Most Beautiful Pretend Game Ever Played

Mathematics is sublime—but it is also make-believe. Its truths are conditional: if these axioms, then those conclusions. When physicists write the cosmos in equations, they are translating mystery into grammar. The translation is elegant, but it is not the thing itself.

To claim that “the universe is mathematical” is to commit linguistic idolatry. Numbers describe patterns; they do not explain being. The formula E=mc² predicts the behavior of matter and energy—it does not tell us what matter or energy are. The certainty of mathematics is the certainty of definition, not of reality.

Einstein himself warned against this confusion: the moment mathematics becomes certain, it ceases to refer to the world. The moment it refers to the world, it ceases to be certain.

4. The Mirage of Empirical Authority

Modern physics and cosmology are cathedrals built on inference. Dark matter, dark energy, singularities, strings—none of these have been seen. They are invoked to preserve the internal coherence of equations that cannot account for observed phenomena. These invisible entities are not discoveries but placeholders for ignorance, named and worshipped as though naming made them real.

The irony is exquisite: in fleeing metaphysics, science reinvented it. It simply changed the vocabulary. Where theologians spoke of the divine, cosmologists now speak of the singularity; both point to something unobservable that explains everything else.

5. Consciousness: The One Fact That Cannot Be Denied

All observation presupposes an observer. Before there is data, there is awareness. Before there is theory, there is experience. To reduce consciousness to neural noise or quantum computation is to saw off the branch upon which knowledge sits.

Science studies phenomena within consciousness while pretending to stand outside it. But consciousness is the condition of the entire enterprise—the light by which all “facts” are seen. Without it, there is no experiment, no equation, no universe as such.

Thus, consciousness is not an afterthought of matter but its precondition. Every attempt to explain awareness as an emergent property of blind particles is a failure to recognize that “blind particles” are themselves ideas appearing in awareness.

6. The Human Element: Experts, Priests, and Pretenders

The “expert” class often claims to speak for reality itself, as though a PhD confers divine insight. Yet their authority rests on consensus, not revelation. Peer review replaces peer thinking; specialization rewards obedience over insight.

Academia has become a hierarchy of sanctioned ignorance—brilliant minds confined to narrow tunnels, mistaking the light at the end for the sun. Their jargon is a fortress built to defend not truth but prestige. To question them is to be labeled “unscientific,” a modern form of heresy.

But no title or theorem exempts a human from the same fleshly frailty that binds us all. Every calculation, every cosmological model, is written by a primate briefly conscious on a tiny planet, staring into an abyss and mistaking its own reflection for the infinite.

7. Conclusion: The Return to Wonder

Science is a method. Reality is an experience. To confuse the two is to turn curiosity into creed. The universe does not speak in equations; it speaks in being.

The humility proper to inquiry is not the arrogance of certainty but the recognition that the map will never become the territory. Our instruments may refine the contours of what is measurable, but the immeasurable remains—the mystery that births both observer and observation.

No one disputes the practical applications of science, utility is not contested. The task is not to abolish science, but to restore perspective: to remember that the finger pointing to the moon is not the moon, and that the most perfect formula will always fall short of describing the fact that anything exists at all.

Reality cannot be owned by a discipline, only encountered by a consciousness.

Why It Is Impossible to Produce Indisputable Evidence That Nature Is Not Infinite

1. You cannot prove non-existence beyond observational horizons.

Physics is bounded by observational limits:

Cosmic horizon

Particle horizon

Measurement precision

Quantum decoherence boundaries

Anything outside these horizons is not empirically accessible even in theory.

Thus, any claim of a “finite Nature” requires absolute knowledge of what lies beyond all possible observation — which is impossible.

You cannot prove a boundary you cannot detect.


PS. Religion(s)/god/gods = pure fiction.
